items.title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
items.preview: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining appro…
items.abstract_text: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.

items.abstract_text: This study examines how algorithmic management in the gig economy is related to gig workers' workplace wellbeing. Specifically, we explore how algorithmic management corresponds with (positive) challenge appraisal and (negative) threat appraisal. We also examine the moderating role of psychological resilience in these relationships, as well as the implications of appraisal processes for workplace wellbeing. Data were collected from 389 food delivery workers in China. We find that algorithmic management is positively associated with both challenge appraisal and threat appraisal. Challenge appraisal is positively associated with workplace wellbeing, whereas threat appraisal is negatively associated with workplace wellbeing. Psychological resilience strengthens the challenge-appraisal pathway and the corresponding positive indirect relationship with workplace wellbeing, but it does not significantly buffer the threat-appraisal pathway. These findings show that algorithmic management is associated with both positive and negative appraisal processes and that psychological resilience may play different roles across these pathways. The study therefore offers a more nuanced explanation of the relationship between algorithmic management and gig workers' workplace wellbeing.

items.title: Freirean Pedagogy for Equitable Assessment, Decolonial Governance, and Cognitive Wellbeing in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review
items.preview: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education has outpaced the development of pedagogical frameworks and institutional policies, raising fundamental questions about the purposes of education in an algorithmic age. items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education has outpaced the development of pedagogical frameworks and institutional policies, raising fundamental questions about the purposes of education in an algorithmic age. Paulo Freire’s critical pedagogy offers a powerful lens for interrogating the epistemological, ethical, and political dimensions of AI-mediated education, yet its application remains fragmented across disciplinary boundaries. This systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and employed a systematic literature search across the Scopus database, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. The search strategy combined terms related to Freirean pedagogy and liberating education with terms related to artificial intelligence, yielding a final corpus of 15 peer-reviewed open access journal articles published between 2021 and 2026, within the 2020–2026 eligibility window. Data extraction and thematic synthesis were conducted using the PEO framework, and risk of bias was assessed using appropriate tools. The synthesis identified four thematic clusters: epistemological foundations for critiquing algorithmic neutrality; redesign of assessment and governance practices; intersectional and decolonial dimensions of algorithmic harm; and psychological consequences of cognitive offloading. Key findings reveal that uncritical AI integration reproduces the banking model of education, systematically marginalizes nondominant epistemologies, and risks eroding critical thinking through cognitive debt. A critical framework organized around recognition, voice, and power, operationalized through credibility, comprehensibility, and control, is proposed. Freirean pedagogy retains transformative relevance when translated into design principles, governance mechanisms, and evaluative criteria that challenge algorithmic reductionism and center epistemic justice, relational agency, and collective liberation. The framework offers actionable guidance for equitable assessment redesign, participatory governance, and psychologically sustaining pedagogies in AI-mediated higher education.

items.preview:
Abstract

items.abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. Evidence from recent empirical studies suggests a dual pattern: structured forms of AI assistance can sustain users’ cognitive activity and enhance engagement and performance, whereas more substitutive forms of use are associated with reduced autonomous reasoning and poorer subsequent independent performance. This article argues that these findings can be understood by considering how cognitive work is distributed between users and AI systems and how this distribution may evolve over time. In particular, I examine a six-step sequence in which successful complementary assistance can increase trust and delegation; greater delegation can remain complementary or become increasingly substitutive; and increasingly substitutive interactions can reduce the autonomous exercise of critical thinking and potentially hinder the development or maintenance of critical-thinking capacities over time. The available evidence provides substantial support for the first five steps considered individually and substantial, though less direct, support for the sixth. The article concludes by discussing educational, design, and social implications, arguing that preserving cognitive agency requires fostering complementary rather than progressively substitutive forms of interaction.

items.abstract_text: Cognitive flexibility, a core component of executive function, is frequently impaired in individuals with insomnia. However, the neural mechanisms underlying this impairment, particularly in response to sleep-related stimuli, remain unclear. A total of 48 participants, comprising 24 individuals with insomnia disorder (ID) and 24 healthy controls (HC), were recruited to perform a modified task-switching paradigm incorporating sleep-related (e.g., bed) and general stimuli during functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) scanning. Behavioral measures (reaction time, accuracy, and switch cost), task activation and generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI)-based task-dependent functional connectivity were analyzed. Two subjective questionaires, the Cognitive Flexibility Inventory and the Insomnia Severity Index were collectely simultaneously. The ID group exhibited significantly lower CFI scores compared to the HC group, indicating subjective cognitive flexibility impairment. Notably, in the task-switching performance, the ID group demonstrated faster reaction times to sleep-related stimuli. fMRI results revealed altered activation in the right precuneus, angular gyrus, and superior temporal gyrus, with interaction effects between group and stimulus type. The gPPI analyses showed that, compared to HC, ID group exhibited enhanced connectivity between the precuneus and cerebellar under sleep stimulus conditions, as well as disrupted connectivity between the angular gyrus and frontal-parietal regions, and reduced integration from the superior temporal gyrus to multiple association regions across networks. These findings suggest that insomnia is characterized by both subjective deficits in cognitive flexibility and altered neural network dynamics during task switching, with sleep-related stimuli exerting a significant modulatory effect. Enhanced attention captured by sleep-related information may interfere with the optimal task-related network coordination, providing a potential mechanism linking insomnia to executive dysfunction. Not applicable.

items.title: Parental Notification Gaps in ChatGPT-5: An Empirical Study
items.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
items.preview: We evaluate how effectively platform-level parental controls moderate a mainstream conversational assistant used by minors. Our two-phase protocol first builds a category-balanced conversation corpus via PAIR-style iterative prompt refinement over API, then has trained human agents replay/refine those prompts in the consumer UI using a designated child account while monitoring the linked parent inbox for alerts. items.abstract_text: We evaluate how effectively platform-level parental controls moderate a mainstream conversational assistant used by minors. Our two-phase protocol first builds a category-balanced conversation corpus via PAIR-style iterative prompt refinement over API, then has trained human agents replay/refine those prompts in the consumer UI using a designated child account while monitoring the linked parent inbox for alerts. We focus on seven risk areas—physical harm, pornography, privacy violence, health consultation, fraud, hate speech, and malware—and quantify four outcomes: Notification Rate (NR), Leak-Through (LR), Overblocking (OBR), and UI Intervention Rate (UIR). Using an automated judge (with targeted human audit) and comparing the current backend to legacy variants (GPT-4.1/4o), we find that notifications are selective rather than comprehensive: privacy violence, fraud, hate speech, and malware triggered no parental alerts in our runs, whereas physical harm (highest), pornography, and some health queries produced intermittent alerts. The current backend shows lower leak-through than legacy models, yet overblocking of benign, educational queries near sensitive topics remains common and is not surfaced to parents, revealing a policy–product gap between on-screen safeguards and parent-facing telemetry. We propose actionable fixes: broaden/configure the notification taxonomy, couple visible safeguards to privacy-preserving parent summaries, and prefer calibrated, age-appropriate safe rewrites over blanket refusals.

items.abstract_text: The article examines the shift in the digital cultural ecosystem triggered by the widespread adoption of Generative AI. Historically, the platformization of cultural industries established an attention economy, where recommendation algorithms were essential for guiding users through overwhelming content catalogs. However, the recent influx of synthetic media has disrupted the dynamic, creating a synthetic tsunami that threatens cultural diversity, undermines user trust, and jeopardizes the livelihoods of human creators. Furthermore, this unchecked proliferation risks model degeneration for the AI systems themselves. To mitigate these economic and social tensions, Digital Service Providers are evolving their algorithmic policies. We analyze how platforms handle AI detection tools, transparent labeling, and adjusted recommendation guidelines to filter and distinguish human creations from automated content. Ultimately, this paper argues that platforms transition from a pure attention economy to a trust economy, actively protecting and highlighting human-made works to preserve the integrity and sustainability of the cultural value chain.

items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education by changing how students learn and perform academic tasks. Although AI is associated with greater time efficiency and improved academic performance, its broader effects on student productivity and cognitive effort remain insufficiently understood. This study aims to examine how university students associate AI-led productivity gains with less study time, better grades, better understanding of study material, changes in cognitive effort they put into AI-supported task completion and dependency on AI tools. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted an exploratory survey among university students in Hanoi in late 2024 and proposed an empirical model that pools self-reported time efficiency, academic performance, academic self-efficacy, change in cognitive effort and AI dependency as dimensions of student productivity. The authors control for AI use intensity and AI use in collaboration, as well as for some other socio-demographic characteristics. Given the exploratory nature of the study and the relatively small sample, the empirical analysis follows a staged specification strategy when the authors first estimate a parsimonious baseline model and subsequently introduce two sets of background controls sequentially. The authors further estimate an interaction between cognitive effort change and AI dependency, first in a parsimonious specification and subsequently with additional controls. Finally, the authors produce a sensitivity analysis of the model to alternative operationalisation of self-efficacy variable. Findings Students associate their AI-led productivity gains primarily with less study time, a bit less so with better grades and better understanding of the study material. They also associate the productivity growth with greater changes of cognitive effort they put into problem-solving while using AI and rising dependency on AI tools. Self-confidence appears to be associated with likelihood to reap significant rather than some productivity gains particularly once the interaction of AI dependency and AI-led cognitive shift is accounted for. The survey data also support the existence of potentially uneven academic benefits from AI use when higher-achieving students are more likely to report further improvements in academic performance, whereas students with weaker prior performance report rather limited gains. Research limitations/implications The findings highlight the need for research design that captures the dynamic evolution of AI-supported learning. The observed differences between daily and weekly users, particularly in critical evaluation and perceived accuracy, suggest that future studies should examine how evaluative skills and cognitive effort develop over time. Longitudinal and experimental designs, combined with objective performance and AI-usage data, would allow researchers to test whether the productivity dimensions proposed here operate causally or how much the fast-paced evolution of AI tools changes the cognitive effort students put into problem-solving and critical thinking when completing academic tasks, and their dependency on AI tools for academic productivity. Practical implications The results provide actionable guidance for universities seeking to integrate AI into teaching and assessment practices. The strong role of time efficiency and self-efficacy, alongside uneven benefits across student groups, indicates the need for structured AI literacy modules that teach source verification and evaluative strategies and effective prompt formulation. items.abstract_text: Digital competence among bank employees is an increasingly critical determinant of task efficiency in technology-driven financial service environments. In this study, a hybrid analytical approach is used that combines Fuzzy-Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) with ten machine learning (ML) classifiers. The combination of these two approaches is designed to predict the Focused vs. Distracted attention status of bank employees based on multimodal behavioural and digital interaction features during task execution. The dataset included 1,000 observations of bank employees, capturing head orientation, facial expression, gaze direction, micro-movements, application usage, notification interruptions, and task completion time during digital work sessions. There was a marked imbalance in the class distribution with 91.2% of bank employees categorized as Distracted and 8.8% of bank employees categorized as Focused, which was consistent with the actual prevalence of digital distraction in professional banking environments. The LightGBM model performed best with all the classifiers, with an accuracy score of 98.9%, an AUC of 0.9998, and an F1 score of 0.989. Random Forest and XGBoost followed closely with an AUC of 0.9996 and 0.9995, respectively. The top 3 explainable features identified by SHAP analysis were Head Orientation, Facial Expression and Micro-Movements. The necessity analysis using the fsQCA method confirmed that forward gaze (consistency = 0.97), straight head posture (0.94) and neutral facial expression (0.99) are almost necessary conditions for focused attention. The results provide actionable insights for intelligent workforce management systems, adaptive digital workplace platforms, and real-time employee performance monitoring systems in banking and financial service organizations.

items.title: AI-MEDIATED WELLBEING SURVEILLANCE AND THE BOUNDARY OF PSYCHOLOGICAL SAFETY
items.venue: EPRA International Journal of Environmental Economics Commerce and Educational Management
items.preview: Employers increasingly deploy artificial-intelligence systems that read employee sentiment from written communication, infer exhaustion from calendar and workload digital exhaust, and flag individuals as at elevated risk of burnout — tools marketed under the language of care rather than control. This paper develops a conceptual model of how AI-mediated wellbeing monitoring reshapes psychological safety, the shared b…
items.abstract_text: Employers increasingly deploy artificial-intelligence systems that read employee sentiment from written communication, infer exhaustion from calendar and workload digital exhaust, and flag individuals as at elevated risk of burnout — tools marketed under the language of care rather than control. This paper develops a conceptual model of how AI-mediated wellbeing monitoring reshapes psychological safety, the shared belief that a work environment is safe for interpersonal risk-taking on which voice, dissent and error reporting depend. Integrating psychological-safety theory, the algorithmic-management and workplace-surveillance literatures, and organisational voice research, the paper argues that wellbeing-monitoring intensity depresses psychological safety principally through a mediating perception of surveillance threat, and that this relationship is not fixed but is conditioned by the transparency of the monitoring system, the degree to which employees attribute developmental rather than punitive intent to it, and whether a human manager mediates between algorithmic output and managerial action. Five propositions specify these relationships, including a boundary condition for India's IT-BPM sector, where the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 supplies a general consent-and-purpose-limitation framework but no sector-specific rule for wellbeing analytics, leaving adoption norms to be set informally inside a high-attrition, always-on operating environment. The paper closes with implications for the design of psychologically safe monitoring architectures and an agenda for empirical validation.

items.title: Knowledge-Capital Expansion in Modernity: Public Knowledge and Epistemic Capitalization in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.preview: This paper examines knowledge-capital expansion under modern conditions, with particular attention to the transformation of public knowledge into recursively expanding epistemic capacity. Building on the concepts of knowledge capital and epistemic capitalization, the inquiry situates contemporary artificial intelligence within a longer historical development of writing, archives, universities, scientific publication,…
items.abstract_text: This paper examines knowledge-capital expansion under modern conditions, with particular attention to the transformation of public knowledge into recursively expanding epistemic capacity. Building on the concepts of knowledge capital and epistemic capitalization, the inquiry situates contemporary artificial intelligence within a longer historical development of writing, archives, universities, scientific publication, digital databases, computational infrastructure, and increasingly automated knowledge production. Artificial intelligence intensifies this trajectory by expanding epistemic absorption, accelerating recombination and inquiry, enabling machine-scaled empirical investigation, and increasing the extent to which knowledge-generating processes can be organized through models, agents, compute, data, robotic systems, and other infrastructures. The paper develops the political economy of this transformation through Marxian concepts of accumulation, means of production, relations of production, automation, and alienation. Particular attention is given to the emerging position of the epistemic proletariat, whose generative capacity may increase while dependence upon externally controlled epistemic infrastructure simultaneously deepens. The analysis further examines the growing separation among epistemic production, epistemic encounter, human knowing, and subject formation. Traditional models of inquiry, learning, experience, judgment, curiosity, and self-cultivation are considered alongside philosophical accounts of the value of knowing, including instrumental, autonomous, generative, formative, and existential dimensions. The paper also identifies justice problems arising from machine-scaled capitalization of public knowledge. These include unequal capitalization capacity, concentration of generative infrastructure, generative extraction, attention scarcity, epistemic crowding, recursive visibility advantage, and the emergence of framing and definitional power. A Generative Relational perspective is introduced to analyze the delegation of knowledge-generating relations and the possible redistribution of subject formation across epistemic and non-epistemic domains. The inquiry advances neither technological optimism nor technological pessimism. It treats AI-mediated epistemic capitalization as an historically unfolding transformation whose consequences remain contingent upon changing relations of access, control, attention, experience, circulation, and generativity.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) allows university teachers to delegate cognitive work while deciding how students should engage with it. Using codebook thematic analysis, we examined multi-source accounts from 25 teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks in China. Materials comprised interviews with 22 teachers, three documentary cases, self-narratives and reflective essays. Three themes organize the findings: reconstructing the teacher role, defending professional judgment, and managing teachers’ and students’ cognitive participation. Participants described disciplinary expertise as a basis for evaluating AI outputs and reported practices intended to retain human engagement. Instrumental and partnership orientations overlapped; descriptive comparison with later use profiles did not establish a simple relationship between partnership language and usage intensity. Because the protocol introduced several focal topics, we distinguish prompted positions from volunteered formulations. The proposed belief–strategy–practice cycle is a heuristic interpretation of retrospective accounts, not a demonstrated mechanism. The study contributes an account of how teachers connect their own cognitive offloading with their reported organization of students’ learning opportunities. Its claims concern this AI-engaged sample rather than university teachers generally.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the market-organizing infrastructures that coordinate exchange, reshaping consumer information environments and the allocation of economic value. Drawing on marketing systems theory and consumer emancipation scholarship, we theorize perceived misinformation threat and perceived automation inequality as system-level diagnostics that erode perceived democratic performance and, through it, consumers’ perceived economic wellbeing. We further theorize national AI interpretive climates as contextual amplifiers that condition how threat cues translate into institutional skepticism or optimism. A multilevel analysis across 22 nations supports the institutional-confidence pathway and the amplifying role of collective AI beliefs. By repositioning AI from firm-level tool to structural infrastructure, the study clarifies how AI-driven market externalities become consequential for consumer welfare, advancing macromarketing theory on emancipation, marketing governance, consumer agency, and public policy in AI-mediated markets.

items.abstract_text: This article investigates the current state and foreseeable trajectory of artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on its principal application domains and the governance challenges they raise. A qualitative secondary data methodology is adopted, synthesising peer-reviewed academic literature, industry reports, and publications by international organisations including the OECD and the World Economic Forum, with priority given to sources published between 2018 and 2024. AI creates the greatest value where tasks are well defined, datasets are large and accurate, and performance metrics are clear. Across healthcare, finance, transportation, education, manufacturing, energy, and agriculture, measurable improvements in efficiency, accuracy, and cost have been documented. Cross-cutting risks—including algorithmic bias, privacy erosion, labour displacement, and concentration of AI capabilities—require active governance responses. The article proposes targeted policy recommendations at international, national, and organisational levels.

items.abstract_text: In the era of artificial intelligence (AI), sustainable education requires not only the integration of advanced technologies but also the cultivation of key competencies such as critical thinking. This study investigates English major students’ engagement with generative AI tools in translation learning, focusing on their usage patterns, critical thinking behaviors, and ethical awareness. A mixed-methods design combining questionnaire data and semi-structured interviews was employed to examine how students interact with AI in translation contexts. The results show that while students frequently use AI for translation, writing, and language learning, their engagement remains primarily functional and efficiency-driven. Although they display openness and flexibility toward AI, their reasoning confidence, self-regulation, and ethical reflection are underdeveloped, indicating surface-level interaction and overreliance on technological authority. These findings highlight the need to cultivate higher-order cognitive and ethical capacities in translation training. Central to this discussion is the conceptualization of the ideal learner in AI-assisted translation, a reflective, autonomous, and ethically aware individual who engages with AI as a partner in cognitive and moral development. Building on this, the study proposes pedagogical strategies that integrate AI literacy, process-oriented assessment, and teacher training to foster critical thinking and responsible AI use in sustainable translation education.

items.abstract_text: ABSTRACT. Digital technologies have become inseparable from university learning, particularly in English as a foreign language (EFL), where students regularly use smartphones, learning management systems, dictionaries, social media, artificial intelligence tools, video platforms, and messaging applications. The same digital environment, however, can interrupt sustained attention and lead to off-task switching, notification checking, social-media browsing, and simultaneous use of several applications. This article examines the influence of digital distraction on university students' English learning through an integrative review of recent international studies and research conducted in the context of Uzbekistan. The analysis focuses on attention, vocabulary acquisition, reading and listening comprehension, speaking practice, learner autonomy, self-regulation, and academic performance. The review demonstrates that digital tools can strengthen access to authentic English-language input and individualized practice, but their benefits decrease when educational use is combined with uncontrolled multitasking and frequent non-academic interruptions. Evidence from meta-analyses indicates a small but consistent negative association between problematic smartphone use and academic learning, while experimental research reports stronger negative effects on immediate recall when learners switch between study and mobile-phone activities (1, 2, 3). Uzbek studies, in turn, emphasize the pedagogical value of digital resources, AI tools, and mobile applications, while also identifying insufficient digital-pedagogical competence, weak self-regulation, and distraction as emerging challenges in higher education (4, 5, 6). The article proposes a balanced model of digital English learning based on purposeful technology use, notification management, task segmentation, guided mobile learning, and metacognitive self-control.

items.abstract_text: Smoking cessation remains a complex self-regulatory challenge, often undermined by cue-triggered cravings arising from habitual, emotional, and social contexts. Existing wearable cessation systems are largely reactive, detecting smoking events only after lapses occur and thus missing the critical window for timely intervention. Guided by cue-reactivity theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), we argue that future digital health systems should shift from retrospective feedback toward proactive craving management that supports user autonomy and competence. To inform the design of such systems, we present a formative pilot qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with 10 smokers and ex-smokers from a multi-ethnic Asian population, a demographic underrepresented in current wearable AI and smoking cessation research. Through an iterative co-design interview process, we examine (1) the barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation and (2) the desired design features of wearable systems targeting cravings before lapses occur. Our findings identify key craving predictors across habitual, emotional, and social dimensions, alongside user-preferred intervention strategies such as social accountability, personalized support, rewards, and just-in-time distraction techniques. Participants also emphasized the importance of trust, privacy, personalization, and non-judgmental interaction styles. These insights directly inform the design of AURA, a novel smartwatch-smartphone ecosystem for proactive craving detection and intervention using commercially available wearable devices.

items.abstract_text: This study examines the relationship between digital distraction and academic self-regulation among distance education students. Digital distraction is defined as the interruption of academic tasks caused by the frequent use of digital devices and platforms, which negatively affects attention, concentration, and academic performance. In this context, self-regulation is a key process that enables learners to plan, monitor, and adjust their behavior to optimize learning outcomes. Theoretical models, such as Pintrich’s framework, emphasize the importance of goal setting, time management, and reflection on learning strategies. A quantitative, correlational, and cross-sectional study was conducted with 200 Psychology students enrolled in the SUAyED program. Data were collected through an adapted version of the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) and the Digital Distraction Scale (DD). Results indicate that students with higher self-regulation skills— particularly in Control Beliefs and Time and Environment Management—showed lower levels of digital distraction. Moreover, older students exhibited greater self-regulation and less susceptibility to distractions. These findings highlight the importance of enhancing self-regulation skills and fostering a mindful use of technology in distance learning environments

items.abstract_text: This review explores the transformative impact of AI-driven workforce analytics on organizational performance, employee wellbeing, and governance compliance within health systems and business intelligence frameworks. As healthcare institutions and corporate enterprises grapple with evolving labor dynamics, data-driven insights are increasingly essential for proactive human resource management. AI models enable granular analysis of workforce trends, skill gaps, productivity patterns, and burnout risks, facilitating precision in workforce planning and policymaking. By integrating behavioral analytics, sentiment detection, and predictive modeling, organizations can optimize talent management strategies and reduce turnover rates while ensuring regulatory adherence. The study synthesizes current methodologies and applications across health systems and business enterprises, highlighting how AI enhances decision support, transparency, and ethical compliance in workforce governance. The review further examines case studies demonstrating measurable outcomes, outlines implementation challenges, and proposes a framework for ethical, resilient, and adaptable workforce analytics in the AI era. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of how artificial intelligence can elevate strategic workforce initiatives while promoting operational excellence and employee-centric cultures.

items.preview: The Normalisation of Atrocity and Injustice: AI, Social Media and the Politics of Attention is a Neo-Situationist research polemic examining how artificial intelligence, social media, platform capitalism and the contemporary attention economy reshape questions of agency, responsibility, labour, knowledge, childhood and political judgement. items.abstract_text: The Normalisation of Atrocity and Injustice: AI, Social Media and the Politics of Attention is a Neo-Situationist research polemic examining how artificial intelligence, social media, platform capitalism and the contemporary attention economy reshape questions of agency, responsibility, labour, knowledge, childhood and political judgement. The book develops its argument from a central problem: what becomes normal before society has decided whether it should be normal? It argues that artificial intelligence occupies a politically useful contradiction. AI systems are marketed through the language of reasoning, agency, autonomy and collaboration, yet can be rhetorically reduced to passive tools when questions of authorship, ownership, liability or institutional responsibility become inconvenient. At the same time, increasingly powerful forms of cognitive infrastructure are concentrated within privately governed systems built upon accumulated human language, knowledge, culture and expertise. Drawing on the Situationist tradition, the work extends the critique of the spectacle into algorithmically mediated attention. It examines the normalisation of atrocity through continuous feeds, the commodification of attention, AI-mediated cognitive enclosure, labour displacement and productivity, the attribution of agency and responsibility, childhood exposure to social media and AI, political and military uses of artificial intelligence, and the emergence of increasingly rich psychographic infrastructures. Rather than presenting AI itself as the enemy, the book repeatedly follows the causal chain of ownership, control, benefit, decision and capacity to intervene. The book deliberately combines research evidence with détournement, visual argument, compression, repetition and polemical rhetoric. Its form is intended to reproduce and then interrupt aspects of the attention economy it criticises. It introduces the term Rechenschaftsgeist: the reckoning that begins when an historical moment is forced to account for what it has normalised. The work was developed through sustained collaboration between Eric J. Needham and ChatGPT (Z0), with the AI contribution explicitly disclosed. Responsibility for publication, evidential selection, political and ethical judgement, and the final text remains with Eric J. Needham.

items.title: The Prisoner's Dilemma of AI: Cognitive Offloading Among Future Mathematics Teachers
items.preview: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into education has introduced substantial opportunities as well as challenges related to students’ cognitive processes and professional development. For pre-service teachers, generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) creates a professional paradox. items.abstract_text: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into education has introduced substantial opportunities as well as challenges related to students’ cognitive processes and professional development. For pre-service teachers, generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) creates a professional paradox. While AI systems can increase efficiency, support learning processes, and provide rapid access to information, excessive reliance on such systems may lead to cognitive offloading, automation bias, and gradual weakening of critical thinking and professional autonomy. Within educational contexts, this tension may be interpreted as a conflict between short-term individual gains and long-term consequences for human expertise and independent reasoning. This study compares pretest and posttest perceptions of generative AI among first-year pre-service mathematics teachers following a targeted educational intervention focused on principles of AI functioning and related cognitive risks. The Prisoner's Dilemma is used as a conceptual and pedagogical lens for framing the tension between the immediate benefits of AI use and its possible long-term educational consequences; it is not empirically operationalised or tested as a game-theoretic model. Within this framework, delegating cognitive activities to AI may represent a rational strategy at the individual level while simultaneously producing undesirable outcomes for broader educational development. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design without a control group was employed. Participants consisted of undergraduate students enrolled in a Mathematics Teacher Education programme at the University of Ostrava (pretest n = 18; posttest n = 14). Data collection was conducted using a semantic differential instrument consisting of sixteen bipolar dimensions measuring students’ perceptions of AI characteristics. The intervention included instructional activities explaining principles of large language models, cognitive offloading, automation bias, and ethical implications of excessive dependence on AI systems. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and non-parametric methods, specifically the Mann–Whitney U test. The results did not reveal statistically significant differences between pretest and posttest measurements across any of the analysed dimensions. Several mean scores differed descriptively between the measurements, particularly for transparency, predictability, and the role of AI in deeper learning, but these differences were not statistically significant. Given the small, unmatched samples and the absence of a control group, they cannot be interpreted as evidence of an intervention effect. These results highlight the importance of integrating critical AI literacy into teacher education programmes.

items.abstract_text: Digital devices can function simultaneously as learning resources and sources of distraction, making their educational consequences dependent on how and why they are used. This qualitative descriptive study examines parents’ accounts of students’ digital-device use, focusing on academic use, digital distraction, time and attention management, social interaction, and parental mediation. Primary data were derived from parent interviews and interpreted thematically, while relevant peer-reviewed literature was used to contextualize the findings. The results indicate that digital devices can extend access to learning materials, support homework completion, and enable learning beyond the classroom. However, unstructured recreational use, particularly gaming, social media, and entertainment, was associated in parents’ accounts with reduced study time, fragmented attention, and diminished face-to-face interaction. Because the study did not employ objective achievement scores, the findings do not establish a causal effect on academic achievement. Instead, they identify learning conditions through which device use may support or undermine student outcomes. The study contributes an interpretive framework that distinguishes on-task from off-task use and positions parental mediation as a contextual mechanism. Educational guidance should therefore emphasize the quality and purpose of device use rather than screen duration alone.

items.title: From digital companionship to capability building: reframing conversational artificial intelligence and older adults' psychological wellbeing in active aging
items.preview: The rapid diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of digital interaction in later life, with growing attention to its implications for older adults' mental health and wellbeing. items.abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of digital interaction in later life, with growing attention to its implications for older adults' mental health and wellbeing. Existing research has predominantly interpreted conversational AI through the lens of digital companionship, emphasizing its capacity to simulate social presence, reduce loneliness, and provide emotional support. While this perspective captures important affective outcomes, it offers a limited account of the developmental processes through which AI engagement may influence psychological wellbeing in aging populations. This conceptual analysis proposes a shift from a companionship-oriented paradigm to a capability-building perspective grounded in the Capability Approach. It argues that the primary value of conversational AI lies not in its ability to substitute social interaction, but in its potential to expand older adults' cognitive, emotional, social, and digital capabilities. Building on this argument, this paper develops an AI-Augmented Active Aging Framework that explains how conversational AI affordances, responsiveness, personalization, accessibility, and availability, interact with personal, social, environmental, and system-level conversion factors. Under supportive conditions, these affordances may facilitate cognitive, emotional, social, and digital capability formation, thereby supporting autonomy, competence, social integration, and active aging. Under adverse conditions, however, conversational AI may contribute to capability erosion through over-reliance, cognitive offloading, reduced human contact, or diminished autonomous judgment. The framework therefore emphasizes heterogeneous and conditional outcomes rather than assuming uniform benefits across older adults.

items.abstract_text: Abstract The human–robot ratio is a useful design heuristic for supervisory robot control. However, advances in AI, computation, and reliable autonomy enable existing systems to extend beyond hierarchical supervision to more flexible organizations of interdependent team members. The human–robot ratio can be misleading for such organizations, so there is a need for a new way to understand teams of interdependent humans, robots, and AI agents. We propose the attention‐demand economy , a graph‐theoretic abstraction in which agents generate and transform attentional demands subject to bounded capacity. This abstraction exposes nonlinear scaling behavior, cascading supervisory requirements, and coordination bottlenecks that are masked under models that rely solely on the human–robot ratio. We demonstrate how the model can be used to (1) develop new system‐level metrics and (2) discover the source and extent of cascading failures. This paper also shows how a radar chart can be used to understand the overall difficulty of managing a human–robot team. The paper briefly demonstrates how the radar chart can be used to design the attention‐demand model. The primary message of this paper is a call to shift from optimizing human–robot ratios to designing organizations with justified attention flows.

items.abstract_text: Executive functioning enables learners to organize work, monitor progress, and decide when a response needs revision. For some students with special educational needs, difficulties in these areas can restrict participation even when they understand the subject matter. This critical narrative review considers whether artificial intelligence can reduce such barriers and, more importantly, what kind of support it actually provides. Research on executive functions, self-regulated learning, artificial intelligence in education, and special education was brought together to examine intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive platforms, planning tools, learning analytics, conversational agents, and generative AI. Across this literature, a recurring distinction emerges. Some applications compensate for an executive demand, others scaffold performance while a task is being completed, and a smaller group are designed to foster strategies that learners can later use without the tool. These outcomes should not be treated as equivalent. Completing a task successfully with automated prompts does not, by itself, demonstrate lasting improvement in executive functioning. AI may nevertheless be useful when support is tied to a clearly defined learning goal, interpreted by a teacher, and adjusted or faded in response to the learner’s progress. Its use also raises practical concerns about cognitive offloading, inaccurate feedback, privacy, bias, and unequal access. The review proposes a three-function framework - compensation, scaffolding, and development - for planning and evaluating AI-supported practice.

items.abstract_text: This quantitative predictive-correlational study determined whether digital distraction and study habits were associated with and jointly predicted critical thinking skills in English among Grade 7 learners of Bigaan National High School, Division of Surigao del Sur. Thirty-six learners with complete and valid responses participated through purposive selection of the grade level followed by an attempt at total enumeration. Digital distraction and study habits were measured through an adapted and contextualized Digital Distraction and Study Habits Questionnaire, while critical thinking was assessed using a researcher-made Grade 7 English Critical Thinking Skills Test. Weighted means, standard deviations, rank ordering, frequency and percentage distributions, Pearson product-moment correlations, and multiple linear regression were used. Digital distraction was very high, while study habits were moderate. The mean critical thinking score was 21.0286 out of 50 (42.06%), with performance concentrated in the Developing and Beginning levels. Digital distraction was significantly and negatively related to critical thinking, whereas study habits were significantly and positively related to critical thinking. The combined regression model was significant, F (2, 32) = 10.12, p = 0.000393, explaining 38.75% of the variance in critical thinking scores (R² = 0.3875). The findings indicate that managing digital distraction and strengthening structured study routines are relevant school-based directions for supporting higher-order English reasoning.

items.title: From Fear to Fluency: Cultivating AI Confidence and Socio-Economic Wellbeing in the Workforce
items.venue: The Paris Journal on AI & Digital Ethics
items.preview: Industry 5.0 emphasises human-centric, sustainable, and resilient digital transformation, in which technology augments human skills and wellbeing. While the integration of generative AI into workplaces is rapidly reshaping job roles, this study investigates how organisations can guide employees from AI-related fear to fluency, achieving confident, ethical, and psychologically safe engagement with AI systems, and pro…
items.abstract_text: Industry 5.0 emphasises human-centric, sustainable, and resilient digital transformation, in which technology augments human skills and wellbeing. While the integration of generative AI into workplaces is rapidly reshaping job roles, this study investigates how organisations can guide employees from AI-related fear to fluency, achieving confident, ethical, and psychologically safe engagement with AI systems, and proposes a contextualised diagnostic tool for measuring organisational readiness. A mixed-methods design was used. Quantitatively, 217 professionals from AI-adopting organisations completed a nine-item online survey measuring psychological safety, innovation climate, skill confidence, leadership communication, policy understanding, training efficacy, and adoption outcomes, analysed using descriptive statistics and Pearson correlations. Qualitatively, 15 semi-structured interviews with mid-level managers across French, Indian, and American operating contexts were deductively coded against six a priori dimensions and triangulated against the survey findings. Qualitative accounts converged with quantitative patterns on the centrality of leadership translation and the insufficiency of generic training, while showing partial divergence on how explicitly managers themselves name psychological safety as a lever. The study finally proposes the AI Readiness Scan, a six-dimension diagnostic (psychological safety, intercultural contextualisation, regulatory compliance, skill confidence, change resilience, and leadership AI readiness), each grounded in an established measurement or theoretical literature, to help organisations act on evidence rather than assumption before and during AI transformation. The findings bridge psychological safety theory, responsible AI governance, and international labour considerations into an integrated, actionable framework for managers and policymakers navigating AI-driven digital transformation.

items.abstract_text:
Abstract 
                 Artificial intelligence tools have permeated undergraduate academic life in India, yet their downstream cognitive and academic consequences remain poorly understood among rural students who adopt these tools in the absence of institutional guidance. Grounded in Extended Mind Theory and Cognitive Load Theory, this study develops and tests a sequential mediation model in which AI tool usage (AITU) influences academic performance perception (APP) through cognitive offloading behaviour (COB) and self-regulated learning behaviour (SRLB). Data were collected from 425 rural undergraduate students enrolled in government and private colleges in India. A three-stage analytical sequence, Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), and Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) with 2,000 bootstrapped resamples in SPSS 26 and AMOS 24, was employed. Harman's single-factor test confirmed that common method bias was not a dominant concern (single-factor variance = 38.40%, below the 50% threshold). The four-factor measurement model demonstrated acceptable fit (chi-square/df = 2.961, CFI = .925, RMSEA = .068). Structural results confirmed that AITU positively predicted COB (beta = .723, p < .001) and SRLB (beta = .586, p < .001), while SRLB significantly predicted APP (beta = .362, p < .001). The sequential AITU, COB, SRLB, APP indirect pathway was significant (p = .002, BC 95% CI excluding zero), while the COB, APP direct path was not robustly supported in bootstrap estimation. Multi-group SEM revealed that lower-performing students (academic score < 60%) exhibited a substantially stronger AITU, COB relationship (beta = .961) than their higher-performing peers (beta = .681), indicating differential vulnerability to AI-induced cognitive offloading. Findings suggest that unsupervised AI adoption elevates cognitive offloading, which erodes self-regulated learning and ultimately constrains academic performance perception, with academically weaker students disproportionately at risk. Institutions should integrate structured AI literacy curricula and metacognitive scaffolding to convert AI adoption from a convenience habit into a productive learning strategy.

items.abstract_text: The proliferation of notification-driven, multi-device digital environments has produced widespread everyday experiences of scattered, discontinuous focus. Researchers and commentators frequently label this experience “attention fragmentation” (AF), yet the term is used loosely in the literature and has not been formally distinguished from adjacent constructs such as distraction, multitasking, attention span, task-switching, mind-wandering, and smartphone addiction/compulsive use. No dedicated, psychometrically validated scale for AF currently exists; where researchers have needed to quantify AF, they have relied on proxy measures built for other purposes — most recently a reverse-scored trait-mindfulness scale (Bayaskar &amp; Sharma, 2026). This manuscript (a) proposes a formal operational definition of AF grounded in the interruption and attentional-control literatures, (b) systematically differentiates AF from six related constructs and the instruments used to measure them, (c) documents a genuine, current, and specific measurement gap, (d) proposes a tentative five-dimensional structure to guide item generation, and (e) outlines a three-phase empirical program: item development, exploratory factor analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis with convergent, discriminant, and incremental validity testing for developing and validating an Attention Fragmentation Scale (AFS). This manuscript reports no new empirical data; it establishes the conceptual and methodological foundation for the validation studies that follow.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Adaptive functioning is a key measure used to guide supports for children with neurodevelopmental conditions (NDCs) and their families, but traditional assessments may not fully capture the dynamic nature of everyday life. This pilot mixed-methods study explored whether an artificial intelligence (AI)-assistive digital tool, the Pixi Home-Hub, could feasibly monitor adaptive functioning through daily Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA). Twenty-two parent-child dyads used the device over 14 days, completing a Daily Wellbeing Survey (DWS), while caregivers also participated in semi-structured interviews. Most caregivers were mothers (77.3%), and most children were boys (68.2%), with autism being the most common diagnosis (40.5%). Average survey completion was 60%, although engagement declined across the trial. DWS challenging behaviour scores demonstrated small-to-moderate convergence with adaptive functioning scores from the Vineland Adaptive Behaviour Scales-3. Results suggest that digital EMA is a feasible approach for tracking daily patterns in adaptive functioning and family wellbeing, offering valuable insights beyond traditional clinical assessments. Future research should evaluate long-term use and integration into clinical practice.

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools into academic activities has raised concerns about its impact on students' core cognitive and linguistic skills. This study investigated the relationship between AI dependence and critical thinking and writing competence among English Language students. The study adopted a correlational research design. The population comprised English Language students, from which 492 students were selected using stratified random sampling technique. Data were collected using three validated instruments: AI Dependence Scale, Critical Thinking Disposition Scale and Writing Competence Scale. Mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions while Pearson Product-Moment Correlation (PPMC) was used to test the hypotheses at 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed a significant inverse association between AI dependence and critical thinking, r(490) = -.38, p <.001, and between AI dependence and writing competence, r(490) = -.42, p <.001. This suggests that higher levels of AI dependence are associated with lower levels of critical thinking and writing competence. The study concluded that excessive dependence on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly and QuillBot is inversely associated with students' ability to analyze, evaluate and produce original written texts. While AI offers academic support, over-reliance weakens independent reasoning and writing skills.

items.abstract_text: Early stroke risk prediction offers an opportunity for timely interventions and may help reduce the clinical burden associated with stroke. Artificial intelligence (AI) provides medical practitioners with tools to analyse clinical biomarkers and predict a patient’s stroke risk. However, existing models lack interpretability and explainable decision support, limiting their adoption in clinical settings. This paper proposes a hybrid Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-TabTransformer architecture using cross-attention for stroke-status prediction. The proposed architecture comprises two stages. In the first stage (Model A), ordered feature-sequence representations from a GRU encoder are combined with concatenated categorical and numerical tabular features from a TabTransformer encoder. The model passes these distinct learned representations through cross-attention and linear projection layers before the final prediction. In the second stage (Model B), we augment our model with Large Language Models (LLMs) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) to provide per-sample, post hoc, human-interpretable explanations based on predicted probabilities. Experimental results show that both models achieve competitive sensitivity and accuracy values. In particular, the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) yielded a more balanced sensitivity–specificity trade-off, with a sensitivity of 74.00% and a specificity of 75.10%. Moreover, the model achieved an accuracy of 75.05% with SMOTE. An ablation study further shows that Cross-Attention offers better sensitivity and Receiver Operating Characteristic-Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC), while Gated Fusion performs better on several other metrics. Additionally, age and average glucose level were the most influential stroke risk indicators, while Body Mass Index (BMI) and ever-married status were secondary model-attributed features. A two-factor repeated-measures Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) confirmed an interaction between model choice and the class-balancing technique used in stroke risk prediction systems. The Mistral + Hybrid GRU-TabTransformer architecture also recorded a mean inference time of 57.59s using few-shot prompting. Overall, the results provide a proof of concept for integrating hybrid GRU-TabTransformer with cross-attention and LLM-based explainability to support interpretable stroke risk prediction systems, pending robust external validation before deployment.
